entries.title: The NRSC’s Spending Surges for Key Midterm Races
entries.summary: The National Republican Senatorial Committee opened the floodgates after the Supreme Court struck down limits on party committees’ coordinated spending.
entries.content:
The National Republican Senatorial Committee’s spending sharply escalated in August following the Supreme Court’s decision to strike down federal limits capping how much parties could coordinate to spend on their candidates.

The NRSC logged less than $3 million in coordinated expenditures prior to the Supreme Court’s decision on July 30. In its most recent Federal Election Commission filing, the NRSC reported spending almost $46 million for candidates across the county.

The three largest coordinated spending allocations were more than $10 million for Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio, more than $8 million for Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa and nearly $8 million into Michael Whatley’s Senate race in North Carolina.

The committee also spent millions on Senate races for John Sununu in New Hampshire, Mike Rogers in Michigan, Rep. Mike Collins in Georgia and Sens. Susan Collins in Maine, Dan Sullivan in Alaska and Darline Graham in South Carolina.

The NRSC listed the purpose of the expenditures as media or direct mail production.

“The NRSC entered August with a record high cash on hand and invested it in coordinated communications,” spokesperson Joanna Rodriguez told The Washington Sun. “Republicans have already booked more in coordinated media and voter contact than our counterpart even has available in cash on hand.”

The NRSC had a more than $16 million cash-on-hand advantage over the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, according to FEC filings from July.

The DSCC did not increase its spending nearly as much. It spent less than $200,000 before the Supreme Court struck down the limits, and spent just over $1 million after the ruling, according to its most recent filing.

The coordinated spending totals reported to the FEC can represent future ad reservations, vendor contracts, polling, message testing and media training, as well as anything else the committees plan with candidates ahead of Election Day.

Before the Supreme Court ruling, campaign arms like the NRSC could only make coordinated spends of up to $61,800 per House candidate (or $123,600 if the state had only one seat). On the Senate side, the limits in 2024 ranged from $123,600 to almost $3.8 million depending on each state's voting-age population.

The NRSC teamed up with Vice President JD Vance when he was a senator from Ohio to file the lawsuit against the spending limits in 2022.

Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in the 6-3 majority opinion that spending of campaign organizations like the NRSC should be interpreted as an expression of free speech and the limits constituted a “severe infringement” on those rights.

“In light of the other meaningful prophylactic measures available to the Government, and given the severe infringement on First Amendment-protected political speech that ensues from limiting a political party’s spending in support of its candidates, we conclude that the political-party coordinated-expenditure limits are ‘disproportionate’ and are not ‘necessary’ and ‘narrowly tailored’ for the circumvention interest it seeks to protect,” Kavanaugh wrote.

He also wrote that eliminating the spending caps would allow party committees such as the NRSC to “participate more freely and compete more fully in the political process.”

entries.title: Mystics 93, Fever 77: Game Recap
entries.summary: Kiki Iriafen racked up 21 points and 14 rebounds to lead Washington to a road win.
entries.content:
INDIANAPOLIS — Kiki Iriafen scored 21 points and grabbed 14 rebounds to help the Washington Mystics beat Indiana 93-77 and pull within a game of the fifth-place Fever.

Shakira Austin added 20 points with 10 boards for the Mystics (26-16), who are one of three teams just a game behind Indiana (27-15) with two regular-season games remaining. The Fever finish with a home-and-home series on Tuesday and Thursday against the Minnesota Lynx, owners of the WNBA’s best record at 32-10.

Sonia Citron scored 16 points and just missed a double-double with nine assists. Georgia Amoore had 11 points with three 3-pointers.

The Mystics jumped out to a 34-19 lead at the end of the first quarter. They led by as many as 26 before closing the half with a 51-30 advantage. Washington was up 77-61 entering the fourth and never were threatened.

Caitlin Clark scored 25 with five assists and Kelsey Mitchell had 22 points for the Fever. But the All-WNBA backcourt shot a combined 14 of 40 from the floor, including making just 6-of-20 3-pointers.

Fever All-Star center Aliyah Boston encountered foul trouble and scored just seven points on eight shots. And Indiana's bench didn't contribute a point until Raven Johnson's jumper with 4:35 remaining in the third quarter.
entries.author: Associated Press

entries.title: Cardinals 5, Nationals 3: Game Recap
entries.summary: After building a lead, Washington gave up three runs in the eighth inning.
entries.content:
ST. LOUIS — Iván Herrera hit a pair of home runs, and Leo Bernal also homered as the St. Louis Cardinals scored three runs in the eighth inning to come from behind and beat the Washington Nationals 5-3 on Sunday.

Bernal hit his fifth homer of the season off Yovanny Cruz (0-2) after Erik Tolman walked Jordan Walker with two outs in the eighth inning.

Herrera hit his second homer of the game and 18th of the season to tie the game at 3-all after hitting a solo shot in the first inning.

It was Herrera's third career multi-homer game and second this season after going deep twice on June 13 at Minnesota.

Luis Gastelum (5-3) pitched a scoreless eighth inning for St. Louis, and Riley O’Brien pitched a perfect ninth to earn his National League-leading 38th save.

Cardinals starter Quinn Mathews allowed three runs on seven hits and two walks in a career-high seven innings.

Jake Irvin allowed two runs on three hits and had eight strikeouts in 5 1/3 innings for the Nationals.

Brady House singled to right field to leadoff the sixth inning, and Abrams hit his 37th homer of the season to right field to put Washington ahead 3-2. He has 99 RBIs on the season.

The Nationals had a chance to add on when Daylen Lile hit a double down the right field line, but Jordan Walker delivered a perfect throw to third base to retire Lile on a call that was confirmed after Washington manager Blake Butera challenged.

entries.title: All-DMV High School Football Players of Week 4
entries.summary: This weekend’s standouts include a bounce-back star from Quince Orchard and a skilled sophomore from Digital Pioneers Academy.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. This week, we’ll have a volleyball players of the week story on Wednesday, and boys and girls soccer selections Friday. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here. 

With another slate of football games in the books, here are five players who turned in memorable performances in Week 4:

Jaiden Hebron, Senior, Running Back, Quince Orchard

One year ago, Hebron suffered a torn ACL in Quince Orchard’s cross-state showdown against Virginia power Stone Bridge. Now fully recovered, the senior shined in this year’s meeting with the Bulldogs, posting a 127-yard rushing performance as the Cougars extended their yearslong winning streak to 30 games with a 20-6 victory. Hebron burst free for a 42-yard dash late in the fourth quarter, then punched in a short touchdown run moments later to put the game out of reach.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Deylen Jones, Senior, Athlete, Oakton

Oakton’s 4-0 start has become one of Virginia’s most intriguing storylines early this season. The Cougars’ high-powered offense is averaging over 44 points per game and picked up a 32-23 win over Colonial Forge on Friday. Jones, a Harvard commit, has helped power Oakton’s success — the senior eclipsed 200 scrimmage yards and found the end zone four times in Friday’s victory.

Davien Parks, Senior, Linebacker, Anacostia

In Anacostia’s battle for the Southeast Cup against D.C. rival Ballou, Parks delivered a statement performance. The senior linebacker registered five sacks in a 38-0 blowout win as coach Seneca Surles’ team picked up its third straight win after dropping its season opener to Digital Pioneers. Anacostia avenged last year’s 50-0 loss to Ballou with a shutout performance of its own.

Kenaz Sullivan, Senior, Defensive Back, The St. James

The young Strivers, a second-year program loaded with Division I commits, have played as advertised through the first month of the season. Coach Darryl Overton’s team thumped Mount Zion Prep on Friday, 65-0. Sullivan, a four-star Maryland commit, pulled down two interceptions in the victory. The Strivers will look to Sullivan for more defensive fireworks with matchups looming against national powers IMG Academy and St. Frances.

Laroy Williams, Sophomore, Running Back, Digital Pioneers

Williams rushed for 182 yards and three touchdowns on just eight carries as the Pythons handled H.D. Woodson this week, 34-0. The win was a resilient performance for Digital Pioneers, which squandered an early 16-point lead to Theodore Roosevelt last week. With their sophomore running back leading the charge on offense, the Pythons look to contend for the city crown following an 11-win season last year.
entries.author: Noah Ferguson

entries.title: NFL Week 2 Takeaways: What’s Wrong With The Chargers?
entries.summary: Plus, the Bears had a scary Sunday and Ja’Marr Chase made the play of the day.
entries.content:
The second Sunday of the NFL season featured a few key injuries, an early contender for catch of the year and another win from a capable backup. Here are five takeaways from Week 2:

It was a nightmarish day for the Bears. 

On Friday, the Bears proudly proclaimed on X that the team had a clean injury report for the first time since Week 7 of the 2022 season. That luck changed on Sunday.

The Bears lost quarterback Caleb Williams halfway through the fourth quarter of a 9–3 home defeat against the Vikings. Williams, a D.C. native who starred at Gonzaga, went down without contact in the fourth quarter and had to be helped off the field after trying to walk off under his own power.

Bears coach Ben Johnson said after the game that Williams injured his right hamstring and the team will know more on Monday after he undergoes testing.

“I'm actually happy it's nothing with the knee,” Johnson said. “That was my first inclination. But yeah, a hamstring can be pretty damaging as well. We'll see how bad it is tomorrow and we'll go from there. Quickly, you've got to turn the page.”

The injury capped off a rough day for the Bears’ offense. After hanging a franchise-record 59 points on the Panthers last week, Chicago struggled to get anything going against Minnesota. The Vikings’ defense made Williams uncomfortable with constant pressure and finished with three sacks.

Tyson Bagent, Chicago’s backup, went 5 for 9 for 54 yards after replacing Williams. The Bears host the Eagles for Monday Night Football in Week 3, giving Williams an extra day to recover if tests show he can play next week.

Ja’Marr Chase made a highlight grab to keep the Bengals rolling. 

It’s way too early to declare a catch of the year, but Bengals wideout Ja’Marr Chase submitted a strong early candidate on Sunday. Late in the first half of the Bengals’ 20–6 win over the Texans, Chase spun off his defender and hauled in a 32-yard pass, planting his toes in the front corner to the endzone. The highlight grab marked the first of his two touchdowns on the day as Cincinnati moved to 2-0.

https://x.com/NFLonCBS/status/2101736151983816836

“I literally don’t know what I did,” Chase said of the catch. “I couldn’t see the ball for a second and I was fighting just trying to get in position, but by the time I’d seen the ball it was in the light and it came real fast and was an adjustment.”

The Bengals went 6–11 last year in the organization’s first losing season since 2020. Joe Burrow, who missed nine games in 2025 with a toe injury, has emphasized the importance of this season and getting the Bengals back to the playoffs. So far, the team’s offense is clicking and a revamped defense has fared well. Despite losing star pass rusher Trey Hendrickson to the Ravens in free agency, the unit has eight sacks through two games.

What’s wrong with the Chargers? 

Los Angeles was a popular preseason pick to make a deep playoff run this year, especially after it brought in Mike McDaniel as offensive coordinator. But McDaniels’ marriage with quarterback Justin Herbert is off to a rocky start. After a 26-14 loss to the Raiders Sunday, the Chargers are 0-2. It’s the first time in Jim Harbaugh’s head coaching career that one of his teams, college or pro, has started 0-2.

Through two games, Herbert has more interceptions than touchdowns (3 to 2) and his offense is averaging just 14 points per game. Even with young playmakers like running back Omarion Hampton and wide receivers Ladd McConkey and Quentin Johnston, Herbert and McDaniels have struggled to get the unit going.

After Sunday’s game, Herbert called his play "uncharacteristic” and added the team has practiced better than it’s played.

“That’s not good enough and we can’t expect to win games like that when we’re playing like that,” he said. “If we’re not playing up to our standard, that’s on us to fix it.”

With the Bills, Seahawks, Broncos and Chiefs all on the horizon, the Chargers suddenly have little margin for error.

Trey Smack AP - 26263747989274 (5488x3659, AR: 1.50)
The Eagles and Packers had to sweat it out. 

The Titans came close to pulling off the day’s biggest upset. Jalen Hurts found Darius Cooper for a three-yard touchdown with nine seconds left in regulation to lift the Eagles to a 24–20 comeback win in Tennessee. It was a positive ending to a bad day for Hurts, who threw two interceptions and was sacked three times.

Saquon Barkley rushed for just nine yards on four carries after injuring his left arm on the Eagles’ first offensive play of the day. He returned in the third quarter to help Philadelphia fend off the Titans. A field goal gave Tennessee a three-point lead with 1:56 left, but Hurts led the Eagles 62 yards in eight plays to set up the game-winning touchdown.

In New York, another NFC contender was put to the test as the Packers needed overtime to earn a 20-17 win over the Jets. Green Bay trailed 17–7 with 11 minutes left in the fourth quarter before scoring 13 unanswered points to improve to 2–0. Jordan Love threw for two touchdown passes, and rookie Trey Smack (another DMV native) hit the game-winning field goal in overtime to deny the Jets an upset.

“It’s one of those games where you just have to keep fighting,” Love said after the game. “It wasn’t pretty, a lot of that game.”

The Packers were without Micah Parsons, who is still rehabbing an ACL tear he suffered late last season. Two more players joined the injury report Sunday as wide receiver Jayden Reed and right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele went down on consecutive plays. Bako-Bewele injured his knee and didn’t return. Reed injured his neck and was hospitalized, but the team said after the game he has feeling in his extremities.

“Doing much better,” Reed posted to X. “Appreciate all the prayers and support.”

Drew Lock kept the defending champs on track. 

Sam who? The defending champions are 2–0 despite the fact that Sam Darnold has played just five snaps this year. With Darnold sidelined by a glute injury, backup Drew Lock has kept the Seahawks flying. On Sunday, he threw three touchdowns to Jaxon Smith-Njigba in a 31–7 win over the Cardinals.

The Seahawks’ defense seems to have picked up where it left off last year, surrendering just two touchdowns in two games with five sacks and four interceptions.

Lock has completed 73% of his passes, throwing for 422 yards, four touchdowns and zero interceptions. His play has given the Seahawks some leeway with Darnold’s recovery. Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald said on Sunday that Darnold could return to practice as early as this week, but with Seattle facing the winless Commanders and Chargers over the next two weeks there may not be reason to hurry.
entries.author: Alex Schiffer

entries.title: Farmers Are 'Pissed' Over Trump's Moves on Beef and Tariffs
entries.summary: The president has upset a reliably Republican rural voter base ahead of the midterms.
entries.content:
Ryan Marquardt, the vice president of the Iowa Farmers Union, was working at an Iowa State Fair booth when the news broke that the U.S. would import hundreds of thousands of tons of below-market-priced beef from Argentina and Brazil.

“I’ve never seen farmers more pissed,” Marquardt said. “That was the maddest I’ve seen farmers in a long time.”

The decision was one of several actions by the Trump administration that experts and insiders say have dulled enthusiasm for Republicans among rural voters, who are already facing high input costs from the war in Iran and escalating trade wars with some of the country’s biggest buyers of American agriculture.

Republicans also control Congress, but have struggled to pass a long-awaited farm bill that farmers say is desperately needed.

Republicans have relied on rural voters to form a solid piece of their base in recent elections, and some argue that the Democratic brand is too poor to rehabilitate in many areas. However, experts still see rural voter apathy as a major issue for Republicans. Even if it doesn't chip away at a crucial voting bloc in some key statewide races this cycle, it could cost the party down the road in a post-Donald Trump future. 

“A lot of people who are now being called ‘reliable Republican voters’ weren’t within living memory,” said William A. Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution.

“It takes something big to change long-established voting patterns, but I think there’s a possibility that the Trump administration has done things that are big enough and bad enough from the standpoint of rural America to make some of the voters who shifted a decade ago reconsider their choice,” Galston said.

Trump’s decision in August to import beef was meant to lower prices, but it sent a shock through American ranchers, who are at their lowest herd counts in decades. Beef prices have risen to record highs, and many producers have begun the long process of rebuilding their herds to meet demand.

Trump also entered an increasingly escalating trade war in August with Canada, a major trading partner. Canada is one of the largest buyers of American agriculture, and experts expect the country to seek imports elsewhere if tariffs make American products too costly.

“Our economies are intertwined on purpose,” John Hansen, the president of the Nebraska Farmers Union, said. “You cannot shoot either Canada or Mexico in the foot without your own foot bleeding.”

Trump’s approval rating fell by 22 percentage points among rural voters from July to August, before his administration announced its intention to import 300,000 pounds of beef and Canada responded with its own tariffs on American goods.

Galston believes that recent data shows a depressed Republican electorate in rural America, one that is still looking for the end of the war in Iran and relief from trade wars that have raised the costs of importing essential materials and made it more expensive to trade in foreign markets.

“He keeps on promising that things are going to get better abruptly,” Galston said. “The timing of the abrupt shift for the better keeps on getting pushed backward, but the shape of the promise remains the same. Eat your spinach today, and there'll be ice cream tomorrow. I think people are no longer willing to believe that.”

Experts and insiders say that the president’s unpopular policies have put races in play in states that Trump carried by double digits in 2024. One Republican consultant who was granted anonymity to discuss campaign discussions pointed to Iowa, where Democrats have leads or remain close in polling across the Senate, governor’s and House races, despite Trump winning Iowa by 13 percentage points in 2024.

The Senate race remains close in Kansas as well, albeit with a Republican advantage, where Trump won by 16 percentage points in 2024. Democrats also lead in polls for the Ohio Senate race, where Trump won by 11 percentage points.

“Rural Americans are feeling the pinch just like everybody else is,” the Republican insider said. “Anytime you raise the cost of goods, that's a bad thing, and so it's going to have an impact on voter apathy or voter excitement.”

Trump’s decisions have sparked backlash among Republicans in both chambers of Congress.

“I’m extremely disappointed by this decision from the White House,” Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Nebraska) said on X. “We all want lower grocery prices, but as I’ve said for months, we cannot do it at the expense of American producers. Flooding the market with foreign beef hurts our livestock industry and undermines the long-term solution: growing the U.S. cattle herd to meet demand.”

Other Republicans, including Sens. Jerry Moran of Kansas, Susan Collins of Maine, Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, as well as Rep. Ron Estes of Kansas, have all spoken out against importing new foreign beef, the new tariffs with Canada or both.

Sen. Jim Risch (R-Idaho), a cattle rancher, spoke out against the White House’s showing interest in importing Argentinian beef a year ago, saying, “If you flood the market, that hurts beef producers badly.”

The Trump administration has tried to tamp down the backlash.

Trump announced an executive order that would give producers additional authority to process and sell their own product, in an attempt to challenge the hold the four largest meat processors have on the industry. Some industry insiders weren’t satisfied with the exchange.

“For us, it feels a little bit more like it's a Band-Aid for a very different kind of wound,” said Jenna Stanton, a policy director for Western Skies Strategies.

Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins has acknowledged the impact of importing beef on America’s ranchers, telling Fox News in an interview that she first heard the news while on her way to Iowa.

“In a way, that was a blessing, because that way I could work to explain the president’s thinking but also hear directly from the ranchers just how difficult that decision was,” Rollins said.

Rollins has had to balance Trump’s desire for lower food prices during an election year when affordability concerns have become a top issue for voters, with an agriculture sector in desperate need of a profit margin.

Rollins has said she believes the current prices for American-produced ground beef are reasonable, but prices still need to go down. On Thursday, she announced a plan for mandatory country-of-origin labeling in part to “protect the American rancher.”

Republicans in Congress are also struggling to use their majority to pass farm policy, most notably the first full five-year farm bill since 2018. The bill advanced from the Senate Agriculture Committee on a party-line vote Wednesday, but its fate on the floor remains uncertain amid a partisan divide over payment shifts in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.

Congress hasn’t passed an updated farm bill since 2018 and has relied on extensions since then to keep essential farm programs running. Farmers are desperate for updated commodity reference prices, which haven’t been updated since inflation worsened after the COVID-19 pandemic.

Trump also took to Truth Social to reaffirm his commitment to passing a farm bill, saying much-needed financial assistance would be on the way. “I want to totally reassure our Farmers and Ranchers, and our Rural Communities, that they will be extremely happy with the end result,” he said.

Weeks before Election Day, Republicans now have to pitch a mixed bag of policies to voters who increasingly view the Trump administration unfavorably. This unfavorability toward Trump may not benefit Democrats, experts say.

Nicholas Jacobs, a professor of American government at Colby College in Maine who has written a book on the voting habits of rural Americans, thinks Democrats have a unique opportunity to make inroads with communities of voters they’ve lost, but isn’t optimistic they will.

“They call the Democratic Party the big tent party,” Jacobs said. “Sometimes I wonder if there’s still room for rural people in that big tent.”
entries.author: Tyler Spence

entries.title: Germany Is Paying the Price for Trump’s EU Feud
entries.summary: Trump’s escalating tariff threats and Chinese competition are crushing Europe’s top exporting country.
entries.content:
BERLIN — Germany’s postwar economy was built for export, but now it’s taking a sizable hit.

U.S. tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump are hurting the sales of the cars and machinery that previously made Germany the most powerful economy in the European Union. Chinese manufacturing competitors are outpacing German companies. And with energy costs rising because of the Iran war, economic analysts and German officials fear the country could slip into a recession.

Feeling the economic strain, some German voters are turning to the political fringes for candidates who promise change, while the country’s leaders — including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz — work to prove they can turn the economy around.

“We’ve seen a longer period of barely any economic growth for a couple of years,” said Melanie Vogelbach, head of international economic policy at the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

Vogelbach called for the German government to address increasing regulatory bureaucracy, an aging population and the rising costs of labor and energy to jump-start the stagnated economy.

“We do have to remember that we do have a lot of structural problems at home that are not necessarily only related to international developments,” Vogelbach said, pointing to high costs, heavy tax burdens and what she called “excessive bureaucracy” that slows down projects and permitting.

As one of the biggest exporters of automotive and manufacturing globally, Germany faces particularly acute economic problems. The Kiel Institute for the World Economy estimated that automotive and manufacturing tariffs levied by the United States could cost the German economy billions in output in the short term.

Experts say the effects of a worsening economy in Germany reveal how much European economies depend on U.S. cooperation. U.S. tariffs have significantly affected German exports, with most German goods facing a 15% baseline tariff, while steel and aluminum are subject to a 50% levy.

The issue came to a head this week when the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, addressed issues with the United States. Speaking to the European Parliament on Wednesday, she said transatlantic relationships faced a “fracture in the international rules-based system.” Von der Leyen also proposed the EU expand its trade agreement with Canada and potentially make it the first associate member of the bloc.

Trump responded by threatening to levy “very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe.”

He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe.”

The German chancellor unveiled a sweeping economic reform package called "Programme for Revival and Employment" on July 2 that aimed to resuscitate Germany's economy by easing bureaucratic burdens and boosting labor market competitiveness. As Germans go to the polls in the coming months, it remains an open question if Merz will emerge with a governing coalition that could pass the economic package.

The stagnant economy appears to be spurring German voters to turn toward far-right parties, such as Alternative for Germany, to solve rising costs, decreasing job opportunities and the slowdown in economic growth.

"When you are worried about your future, when you're worried about having your job in the future, that is something that mostly triggers you or makes you at least open to vote extreme, maybe out of protest," Simon Schütz, a spokesperson for the German Association of the Automotive Industry, told the Washington Sun.

He added: "If you don't take those tough decisions now, you might have to take much tougher decisions in some time. The goal is to work together to make the business model in Germany fit for the future once again. Only in this way will we be able to continue manufacturing here. And only in this way can we safeguard jobs."

Rolf J. Langhammer, a researcher at the Kiel Institute, placed China’s rise in economic power within a broader list of pressures facing Germany: an aging population, lagging digitalization and artificial intelligence adoption relative to the U.S. and China, as well as an incomplete shift to renewable energy.

“Germany, and also the European Union, but Germany in particular, is an aging economy which has profound changes in its production structure, in its demand structure,’ he said.

Schütz framed the tariffs as one more strain on an automotive industry already losing its competitive footing.

"When you look at certain location-side factors such as energy prices, bureaucracy, taxes, regulation — all of this, Europe has kind of lost its base, and other regions went ahead of it," Schütz said.

Langhammer said German lawmakers and officials must figure out how to move forward without relying on the United States.

“Europe must become economically more independent,” Langhammer said, “and rely on its own strength.”
